conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee. You were brought in with severe abdominal pain, fever, and diarrhea. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had watery diarrhea all day, uncountable really, and crampy pain—like 8 or 9 out of 10. It started suddenly, and I had a fever of 102.5. It feels like food poisoning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any blood in the stool? Travel? Or unusual foods?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood, no travel. I didn’t eat anything strange. But my cat has been sick—low energy, dry nose. Could that matter?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, though it’s more likely a viral infection. We’ll run stool tests to check for infections. Your vitals were high in the ER—fever and elevated heart rate—but you’re more stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had nausea for months, especially after eating. It got worse after my last hospital stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your last admission was for nausea and kidney issues. We’ll keep an eye on your kidneys. For now, we’re giving IV fluids and monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your fever has gone down, and the diarrhea stopped. That’s a good sign. But you’re still not eating much, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I tried clear liquids, but I feel full fast and nauseous. Same as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re concerned about gastroparesis—delayed stomach emptying—especially with your diabetes. We’ll consult GI and may do a gastric emptying study.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What causes that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Diabetes can damage nerves that control the stomach. That’s likely what’s happening here. We’ll confirm with a test.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scan came back—no appendicitis, no blockage. Your abdomen looks clear. That supports the idea of a functional issue like gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stool tests were negative for C. diff, parasites, and common bacteria. No sign of infection. The fever and diarrhea were likely a brief viral episode.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But the nausea and fullness are still here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s why we’re moving forward with the gastric emptying study. It will show how fast your stomach empties food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The gastric emptying study is back. It shows delayed emptying—only 61% emptied at 2 hours, and 39% was still in your stomach at 4 hours. That confirms gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I feel so full and nauseous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The stomach isn’t moving food into the intestines properly. We’ll start high-dose Zofran before meals to help with nausea and improve emptying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I ever eat normally again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need to make some changes—smaller, more frequent meals, low-fat, low-fiber, and lactose-free. We’ll give you diet instructions before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve switched you from omeprazole to pantoprazole. It’s similar but may cause less nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my diabetes meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve held your glyburide because you’re not eating well. We’re using insulin shots to manage your blood sugar safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling? Any nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still nauseous, but I tried some toast. It stayed down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’ll keep advancing your diet slowly. Also, you’ve been constipated the last few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had a bowel movement in four days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give a Dulcolax suppository and docusate to help. Constipation can happen with gastroparesis and pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the constipation resolved with the enema. You’re passing stool normally now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better. Can I try more food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll try a full liquid diet today, then soft foods tomorrow. The goal is to get you on a regular diet before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You tolerated the soft diet well. No nausea or vomiting. That’s a big step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still tired, but I’m glad I can eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function is stable—creatinine 1.1, near your baseline. That’s good. We’ll keep you on IV fluids until you’re drinking enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your blood pressure meds. You’ve been missing labetalol doses because of low heart rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel dizzy and tired when I take it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discontinuing labetalol. Your blood pressure is well-controlled on lisinopril, amlodipine, and spironolactone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been on a full diet for a day with no issues. We’re planning for discharge in a couple of days if this continues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What meds will I go home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take lisinopril, amlodipine, spironolactone for blood pressure, simvastatin for cholesterol, and pantoprazole for stomach protection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For gastroparesis, you’ll take ondansetron before meals. And docusate if constipated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No more glyburide?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not for now. Your PCP will decide when to restart it based on your eating and blood sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last night you slept well. No nausea, and you finished your meals. We’re on track for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. But what if the nausea comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take the ondansetron before meals. Stick to small, low-fat meals. Call your doctor if you have severe pain, fever, or can’t keep food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your primary care doctor soon. Keep your GI appointment. They’ll monitor your gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve updated your discharge meds. You’ll get a 30-day supply of pantoprazole and 60 ondansetron tablets.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the inhaler?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep using your Flovent for asthma. It’s unchanged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your last EGD showed a hiatal hernia and mild gastritis. The polyps were likely from long-term PPI use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the polyps are benign. But we’ll monitor them. The hernia may contribute to reflux, so stay upright after eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge. Your condition has improved significantly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Remember: take ondansetron before meals, eat small lactose-free meals, and don’t restart labetalol unless your doctor says so.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And call if I get worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your diet and meds one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll listen carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re doing well. Discharge paperwork is ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy. Rest, follow the diet, and keep your appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already feel better than I have in weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’re glad we could help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another test later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Your GI doctor will decide if further monitoring is needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just keep track of your symptoms and report any changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up as told.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.
